title: Poverty, home-made rhythm and no money for conservatory
summary: He argues poor Southern blacks made music with bones and ran because it was free, and that lack of money kept him from the New England Conservatory.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Politics, race and the state of the country

blocks.x: Then, as you go farther south, the poor people were poorer, and they didn't even have those instruments. I've seen guys make as much music as Gene Krupa or Chick Webb with two bones. They'd just take these two bones and rattle them, clack, clack, clack, and could really to do a dance. So, as far as that goes, they been havin' to do that because we didn't have anything else.

And, in sports, our greatest runners, what do they do. You don't find the black people goin' in much for golf or tennis, or things like that. Because they don't have money to buy the rackets and the golf clubs. But we was great runners. Why?
Because it don't cost you nothin' to run.

You know what I mean? And the sports like running. We were in basketball, or we were in football before we were in basketball, because all you had to do was buy a five cent rocket in those days, and you were in baseball. You could get a stick anywhere to hit the ball.

See, but of course, we didn't have the money. That's the one thing that interfered with a lot of things that we didn't take advanced courses. We couldn't go to the New England Conservatory in those days, because we didn't have the money to do those things.

So, a lot of times, maybe if I had gone to the New England Conservatory, I would have been on the classical kick. But I didn't have any money, I had to get it the best way I could because I certainly didn't want to go into church and play for the church. I didn't want to do that, because I didn't like the church.
